title: The bomb that sank the Rohna
pull: One bomb, kept secret for decades

facts.text: The Henschel Hs 293 was a guided glide bomb: a small winged missile dropped from a bomber, boosted by a liquid fuel rocket that fired for about 10 seconds, then gliding onto a ship.
A crewman in the bomber steered it all the way with a joystick, sending commands over a radio link (the FuG 203 transmitter) while he watched flares or a lamp on its tail.
It was designed at Henschel by a team under Herbert Wagner, and it weighed about 1,045 kg. Its warhead was built from a 500 kg bomb.
Luftwaffe crews first used it in combat on 25 August 1943 against the sloops HMS Bideford and HMS Landguard in the Bay of Biscay. The warheads failed to explode.
On 26 November 1943, about 16:30, Luftwaffe He 177 bombers with Ju 88 escorts attacked convoy KMF 26 off Bougie, Algeria. The He 177s launched a wave of Hs 293s.

Between about 17:15 and 17:25, the He 177 flown by Hans Dochtermann released a glide bomb that struck the port side of HMT Rohna, a British India Steam Navigation troopship carrying American soldiers.
Rohna was the only ship lost. 1,138 men died, 1,015 of them Americans, the largest loss of U.S. troops at sea from enemy action in a single incident.
The minesweeper USS Pioneer, the cargo ship Clan Campbell and the destroyer HMS Atherstone pulled 819 survivors from the dark sea, about 600 of them aboard Pioneer.

The loss was kept quiet. In February 1944 Washington admitted only that more than 1,000 men had died on an unnamed troopship, the ship was not named until 1945, and a fuller account came out only in 1967.
The same weapon sank USS LST-282 off southern France on the evening of 15 August 1944, the first day of the landings there. Army cameramen filmed her burning that night.

photoNote: Tier: green. A captured Hs 293 on a stand in Great Britain, 10 September 1944, side view with wings, tail and the rocket pod slung below. U.S. Army Air Forces photo 342-FH-3A06592-B73172AC (NARA RG 342), public domain. Commons thumbnail 1280 x 1020 (original 3724 x 2968; a 1920 px try hit a Wikimedia error). Runner up: the companion three quarter view, 342-FH-3A06591-A73172AC, not saved, 3744 x 2871 on Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Captured_German_Henschel_Hs_293_glide_bomb_in_Great_Britian,_on_10_September_1944_(342-FH-3A06591-A73172AC).jpg). Spec rows: Carried by (Wikipedia, NASM, National WWII Museum all list He 111, He 177, Fw 200, Do 217); Weight (Wikipedia 1,045 kg, NASM 2,304 lb); Wingspan (Wikipedia 3.1 m, National WWII Museum 10 ft, LRC 310 cm); Warhead (NASM modified SC 500, LRC 500 kg bomb); Guidance (Wikipedia, National WWII Museum, NASM); Rocket boost (Wikipedia, NASM, National WWII Museum). Left out: speed (Wikipedia 260 m/s against NASM 860 km/h), range (Wikipedia 4 to 8.5 km by altitude against Museum 3 to 5 miles), warhead weight (Wikipedia 295 kg against Museum 1,000 lb).
photoCredit: A captured Henschel Hs 293 glide bomb in Britain, 10 September 1944. U.S. Army Air Forces photo, NARA 342-FH-3A06592, public domain.

declassified.fact: Most of Rohna's crew were South Asian lascar seamen. Her serang, the head of the deck crew, Bhowan Meetha, helped launch lifeboats as she sank, and wartime survivor reports later contradicted a 1998 book that blamed the lascars for the losses.

film.shot_notes: First 82 s of the Signal Corps reel (encoded again as H.264). Shot card: night shots from behind a building wall of LST 282 burning after a radio controlled flying bomb released from a German Dornier, about 2100 on D Day; silent. 00:00 to 00:06 NARA logo and black. 00:08 to 01:14 the burning LST at night, flames and smoke silhouetted through trees and a balustrade: strongest bursts 00:12 to 00:28 and 00:52 to 01:08. 01:16 on is the next day's beach (DUKWs), not used. Open on the fire at 00:12. One clear thing happening, so keep it short (15 to 20 s).
film.license: Public domain, U.S. government work (U.S. Army Signal Corps, NARA Record Group 111).
film.date_note: Not the Rohna. This is USS LST-282 burning off southern France on the night of 15 August 1944 after an Hs 293 hit (the shot card says 14 Aug, but the Dragoon landings and the sinking were on 15 Aug). No film of the Rohna exists. Caption it as what an Hs 293 hit did to another Allied ship nine months later.

body:
Hans Dochtermann released one glide bomb over a convoy off Algeria. It killed 1,015 Americans, and the full account did not come out until 1967.

26 November 1943. Luftwaffe He 177s attacked convoy KMF 26 off Bougie late that afternoon and launched a wave of Hs 293s. Dochtermann's struck the port side of HMT Rohna, a troopship carrying American soldiers. 1,138 men died, the largest loss of U.S. troops at sea from enemy action in a single incident.

The Hs 293 was a small winged missile with a 10 second rocket boost and a warhead built on a 500 kg bomb. A crewman guided it over a radio link while watching a light on its tail.

USS Pioneer and two other ships pulled 819 survivors from the dark sea.
